Concept. A cell M[A, a] is filled by the alternative A → α when a ∈ FIRST(α), and by A → ε for every a ∈ FOLLOW(A). Two entries in one cell mean the grammar is not LL(1).

Step by step.

  1. S′ occurs at the very end of S → i E t S S′, so FOLLOW(S′) ⊇ FOLLOW(S) = {e, $}.
  2. FIRST(e S) = {e}, so M[S′, e] receives S′ → e S.
  3. Because S′ is nullable, S′ → ε is entered in every cell of FOLLOW(S′) — and e is one of them.
  4. So M[S′, e] holds both S′ → e S and S′ → ε: the parser cannot tell, from the token else, whether it belongs to the inner or the outer if.

Answer: M[S′, e] — option B.

Common misconception. Expecting the conflict at M[S, i] because the grammar is "about" the two if rules. The clash is on the token else: it is in FIRST(e S) and also in FOLLOW(S′), which is what an ε-production needs.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: For the grammar S → A B, A → a A | ε, B → b B | ε, how many cells of the LL(1) parsing table are non-empty? Count a cell once however many entries it holds. (Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html: For the grammar S → A B, A → a A | ε, B → b B | ε, how many cells of the LL(1) parsing table are non-empty? Count a cell once however many entries it holds. (Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Fill M[A, a] from FIRST for every alternative that begins with a terminal, and place A → ε in every cell M[A, b] with b ∈ FOLLOW(A).

Step by step.

  1. Sets: FIRST(A) = {a, ε}, FIRST(B) = {b, ε}, FIRST(S) = {a, b, ε}.
  2. FOLLOW(S) = {$}; FOLLOW(A) = FIRST(B) − {ε} ∪ FOLLOW(S) = {b, $}; FOLLOW(B) = FOLLOW(S) = {$}.
  3. Row S: M[S, a] = S → A B (from FIRST(A)), M[S, b] = S → A B (A nullable, b ∈ FIRST(B)), M[S, $] = S → A B (both nullable). Three cells.
  4. Row A: M[A, a] = A → a A, M[A, b] = A → ε, M[A, $] = A → ε. Three cells.
  5. Row B: M[B, b] = B → b B, M[B, $] = B → ε. Two cells.
  6. Total 3 + 3 + 2 = 8. No cell holds two entries, so the grammar is LL(1).

Answer: 8 non-empty cells.

Common misconception. Writing A → ε in a single cell labelled ε. The ε-production is duplicated into every terminal of the FOLLOW set — that duplication is exactly what can create a conflict.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: For the grammar S → A B, A → a | ε, B → b | ε, the set FIRST(S) is
questions.question_html: For the grammar S → A B, A → a | ε, B → b | ε, the set FIRST(S) is
options: {a, b}
{a, b, ε}
{a, ε}
options_html: {a, b}
{a, b, ε}
{a, ε}
{a, b, $}
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. For a right side X1 X2 … Xn, add FIRST(X1) − {ε}; add FIRST(X2) − {ε} as well only if X1 is nullable; and add ε only if every Xi is nullable.

Step by step.

  1. FIRST(A) = {a, ε}, so a ∈ FIRST(S).
  2. A is nullable, so FIRST(B) − {ε} = {b} also enters FIRST(S).
  3. Both A and B are nullable, so A B derives ε and ε ∈ FIRST(S).
  4. Hence FIRST(S) = {a, b, ε}.

Answer: {a, b, ε} — option B.

Common misconception. Stopping at the first symbol that has a non-empty FIRST set. The second symbol contributes only because the first is nullable — but it does contribute.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: A recursive-descent parser for an LL(1) grammar must choose one alternative of A when the next input token is x. It chooses the alternative α such that
questions.question_html: A recursive-descent parser for an LL(1) grammar must choose one alternative of A when the next input token is x. It chooses the alternative α such that
options: x ∈ FIRST(α); if no alternative satisfies this and A is nullable, it takes A → ε whenever x ∈ FOLLOW(A).
x ∈ FOLLOW(α) for every alternative α of A.
x ∈ FIRST(A), taking the first alternative listed whenever several qualify.
it tries every alternative in turn and backtracks when one fails.
options_html: x ∈ FIRST(α); if no alternative satisfies this and A is nullable, it takes A → ε whenever x ∈ FOLLOW(A).
x ∈ FOLLOW(α) for every alternative α of A.
x ∈ FIRST(A), taking the first alternative listed whenever several qualify.
it tries every alternative in turn and backtracks when one fails.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. In predictive (LL(1)) parsing the lookahead token must identify the alternative uniquely: the token is either one that the alternative can start with, or — when the alternative is ε — one that may legitimately follow the nonterminal.

Step by step.

  1. If x ∈ FIRST(α) the alternative can begin with x, so expanding it is correct.
  2. If no alternative can begin with x but x ∈ FOLLOW(A), then A must produce nothing here and the parser takes A → ε.
  3. LL(1) guarantees these two tests never both apply and never leave the choice open, so no backtracking is needed (option D is the definition of a non-predictive parser).
  4. FOLLOW(α) (option B) is not defined — FOLLOW is a property of a nonterminal, not of a right side.

Answer: the FIRST test, with the FOLLOW test for the nullable case — option A.

Common misconception. Using FIRST(A) instead of FIRST(α). FIRST(A) is the union over all alternatives, so it cannot distinguish them — which is precisely the information the parser needs.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: The grammar A → a b c | a b d | a e is fully left factored. The result is
questions.question_html: The grammar A → a b c | a b d | a e is fully left factored. The result is
options: A → a A′, A′ → b c | b d | e
A → a A′, A′ → b A″ | e, A″ → c | d
A → a A′, A′ → b A″ | e A″′, A″ → c | d
A → A′ a, A′ → b c | b d | e
options_html: A → a A′, A′ → b c | b d | e
A → a A′, A′ → b A″ | e, A″ → c | d
A → a A′, A′ → b A″ | e A″′, A″ → c | d
A → A′ a, A′ → b c | b d | e
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Left factoring pushes the longest common prefix of two alternatives into a new nonterminal, so that one token of lookahead decides between the remainders. It is applied repeatedly until no two alternatives of the same nonterminal share a first symbol.

Step by step.

  1. All three alternatives begin with a, so factor it once: A → a A′ with A′ → b c | b d | e.
  2. A′ still has two alternatives beginning with b, so factor again: A′ → b A″ | e and A″ → c | d.
  3. Now every nonterminal has alternatives with distinct FIRST sets: FIRST(c) = {c}, FIRST(d) = {d}, FIRST(b A″) = {b}, FIRST(e) = {e}. Factoring is complete.
  4. Option A stops after one step and leaves a FIRST/FIRST conflict on b; option C introduces a needless nonterminal for e.

Answer: A → a A′, A′ → b A″ | e, A″ → c | d — option B.

Common misconception. Factoring only the outer common symbol. A single pass leaves the inner pair b c and b d still ambiguous on b; factoring is applied until no FIRST conflict remains.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: Which of the following transformations leave the language generated by a grammar unchanged? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Which of the following transformations leave the language generated by a grammar unchanged? (Select all that apply.)
options: Replacing A → A α | β, where β does not begin with A, by A → β A′, A′ → α A′ | ε.
Left factoring two alternatives that share a common prefix.
Deleting every ε-production of the grammar.
Deleting useless symbols, that is, non-generating and unreachable symbols.
Reordering the alternatives of a non-LL(1) grammar until it becomes LL(1).
options_html: Replacing A → A α | β, where β does not begin with A, by A → β A′, A′ → α A′ | ε.
Left factoring two alternatives that share a common prefix.
Deleting every ε-production of the grammar.
Deleting useless symbols, that is, non-generating and unreachable symbols.
Reordering the alternatives of a non-LL(1) grammar until it becomes LL(1).
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A transformation is language-preserving when the set of terminal strings derivable from the start symbol is unchanged. Left-recursion elimination and left factoring are such transformations; deleting ε-productions and reordering alternatives are not, in general.

Step by step.

  1. (A) true: A → A α | β generates β αk for k ≥ 0, and so does A → β A′ with A′ → α A′ | ε.
  2. (B) true: factoring only regroups alternatives, it derives exactly the same strings.
  3. (C) false: dropping every ε-production removes ε from the language and breaks every derivation that relied on an optional part; a correct elimination must add compensating productions instead of merely deleting.
  4. (D) true: a symbol that generates no terminal string, or that can never be reached from the start symbol, contributes nothing to the language.
  5. (E) false: reordering alternatives cannot remove a FIRST/FIRST or FIRST/FOLLOW conflict; the ambiguity stays in the grammar. Only rewriting the rules helps.

Answer: options (A), (B) and (D).

Common misconception. Believing every "clean-up" step is safe. ε-elimination is language-preserving only when it is done properly — replicating the nullable symbols into the other right sides — and even then ε is lost unless the start symbol is nullable.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: A predictive parser uses the grammar E → T E′, E′ → + T E′ | ε, T → F T′, T′ → * F T′ | ε, F → ( E ) | id. For the input id + id it applies a sequence of productions. How many productions are applied in total, counting each ε-production that is applied? (Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html: A predictive parser uses the grammar E → T E′, E′ → + T E′ | ε, T → F T′, T′ → * F T′ | ε, F → ( E ) | id. For the input id + id it applies a sequence of productions. How many productions are applied in total, counting each ε-production that is applied? (Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A predictive parser expands nonterminals left to right, and each expansion is the application of exactly one production. The count is therefore the number of nonterminal expansions in the leftmost derivation of the input, including the expansions of the ′-nonterminals to ε.

Step by step.

  1. E → T E′ — 1.
  2. T → F T′ — 2.
  3. F → id, matching the first id — 3.
  4. T′ → ε, since the lookahead is + and + ∈ FOLLOW(T′) — 4.
  5. E′ → + T E′, consuming the + — 5.
  6. T → F T′ — 6.
  7. F → id, matching the second id — 7.
  8. T′ → ε, lookahead $ — 8.
  9. E′ → ε, lookahead $ — 9.

Answer: 9 productions.

Common misconception. Counting only the "visible" productions and dropping the two ε-expansions. Every nonterminal in the sentential form must be expanded, and a nonterminal that disappears by ε still costs one production.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: A grammar is LL(1) if and only if, for every pair of distinct alternatives α and β of a nonterminal A,
questions.question_html: A grammar is LL(1) if and only if, for every pair of distinct alternatives α and β of a nonterminal A,
options: FIRST(α) ∩ FIRST(β) = ∅, and if α ⇒* ε then FIRST(β) ∩ FOLLOW(A) = ∅ (and symmetrically for β).
FIRST(α) ∩ FOLLOW(A) = ∅ for both alternatives.
FIRST(α) ∩ FIRST(β) = ∅ and FOLLOW(A) = ∅.
the grammar contains no ε-production.
options_html: FIRST(α) ∩ FIRST(β) = ∅, and if α ⇒* ε then FIRST(β) ∩ FOLLOW(A) = ∅ (and symmetrically for β).
FIRST(α) ∩ FOLLOW(A) = ∅ for both alternatives.
FIRST(α) ∩ FIRST(β) = ∅ and FOLLOW(A) = ∅.
the grammar contains no ε-production.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The LL(1) condition is exactly the statement that no cell of the parsing table receives two entries. Two ways of colliding are possible: two alternatives can start with the same terminal, or a nullable alternative can vanish on a terminal that another alternative can start with.

Step by step.

  1. FIRST(α) ∩ FIRST(β) = ∅ rules out the first kind of collision: no terminal selects two alternatives by starting them.
  2. If α ⇒* ε, then A → α is entered in every cell M[A, b] with b ∈ FOLLOW(A), so FIRST(β) must avoid FOLLOW(A).
  3. Options B and C are too strong: FOLLOW(A) may be non-empty, it just must not overlap the FIRST sets of the other alternatives.
  4. Option D is false: S → a S b | ε contains an ε-production and is LL(1).

Answer: option A.

Common misconception. Thinking LL(1) forbids ε-productions. It only requires that the ε-alternative be distinguishable from the others by the lookahead, which is what the FOLLOW test checks.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: For the grammar S → A B, A → ε | a, B → b | ε, the set FIRST(B) is
questions.question_html: For the grammar S → A B, A → ε | a, B → b | ε, the set FIRST(B) is
options: {b, ε}
{ε}
{a, b, ε}
options_html: {b}
{b, ε}
{ε}
{a, b, ε}
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. FIRST of a nonterminal is the union of the FIRST sets of its alternatives, taken one production at a time.

Step by step.

  1. B → b contributes b.
  2. B → ε contributes ε.
  3. No other production has B on the left.
  4. Hence FIRST(B) = {b, ε}.

Answer: {b, ε} — option B.

Common misconception. Reading the alternatives of A into FIRST(B), or writing {ε} alone because B is nullable. Nullability adds ε; it does not remove the terminals.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: Which of the following statements about recursive-descent parsing are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements about recursive-descent parsing are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Without memoisation, a backtracking recursive-descent parser can take time exponential in the input length on some grammars.
For an LL(1) grammar one token of lookahead always selects the alternative, so no backtracking is needed.
Recursive descent handles a left-recursive grammar directly, because the recursion in the parser mirrors the recursion in the grammar.
Left recursion must be removed before a recursive-descent parser is written.
A recursive-descent parser builds the parse tree bottom-up, from the leaves to the root.
options_html: Without memoisation, a backtracking recursive-descent parser can take time exponential in the input length on some grammars.
For an LL(1) grammar one token of lookahead always selects the alternative, so no backtracking is needed.
Recursive descent handles a left-recursive grammar directly, because the recursion in the parser mirrors the recursion in the grammar.
Left recursion must be removed before a recursive-descent parser is written.
A recursive-descent parser builds the parse tree bottom-up, from the leaves to the root.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A recursive-descent parser has one procedure per nonterminal, and a procedure calls the procedures of the symbols on the right side of the alternative it chooses. It is therefore a top-down, leftmost-derivation parser, and its control flow copies the shape of the grammar.

Step by step.

  1. (A) true: with backtracking, each failed alternative may re-parse the same suffix, and the number of partial parses can grow exponentially — the classical reason backtracking descent is avoided in production compilers.
  2. (B) true: LL(1) means the parsing table has at most one entry per cell, and a recursive-descent parser implements that table directly.
  3. (C) false: for A → A α | β the procedure for A calls itself before consuming any input, so it recurses forever without making progress.
  4. (D) true: that is why the elimination of Unit-2 left-recursion removal precedes the parser construction.
  5. (E) false: bottom-up parsing (shift-reduce) builds the tree from the leaves; recursive descent builds it from the root downwards.

Answer: options (A), (B) and (D).

Common misconception. Assuming the parser's recursion can "handle" the grammar's recursion. The parser mirrors the grammar, so a left-recursive rule becomes an infinite loop rather than a left-associative parse.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: In the grammar F → ( E ) | id, how many terminals belong to FIRST(F)? (Enter an integer. Do not count ε, since F is not nullable.)
questions.question_html: In the grammar F → ( E ) | id, how many terminals belong to FIRST(F)? (Enter an integer. Do not count ε, since F is not nullable.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. FIRST(F) is the set of terminals that can begin a string derived from F.

Step by step.

  1. F → ( E ) begins with the terminal (.
  2. F → id begins with the terminal id.
  3. Neither alternative is nullable, so ε ∉ FIRST(F).
  4. Hence FIRST(F) = {(, id} — two terminals.

Answer: 2 terminals.

Common misconception. Counting ) or E. ) comes after E and never begins a string of F, and E is a nonterminal, not a terminal.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: For the grammar S → A a | b, A → S d | c, indirect left recursion is removed by substituting the S-productions into A and then removing the immediate left recursion. The resulting productions for A are
questions.question_html: For the grammar S → A a | b, A → S d | c, indirect left recursion is removed by substituting the S-productions into A and then removing the immediate left recursion. The resulting productions for A are
options: A → A a d | b d | c, with no further step needed
A → b d A′ | c A′, A′ → a d A′ | ε
A → b d | c, A′ → a d A′
A → S d | c, unchanged, because the recursion is in S
options_html: A → A a d | b d | c, with no further step needed
A → b d A′ | c A′, A′ → a d A′ | ε
A → b d | c, A′ → a d A′
A → S d | c, unchanged, because the recursion is in S
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Indirect (mutual) left recursion is removed in two stages: substitute the earlier nonterminal's alternatives into the later one, which turns the indirect recursion into an immediate one, and then apply the standard immediate-elimination rule.

Step by step.

  1. Take the order S then A. In A → S d, replace S by its alternatives: A → A a d | b d, together with the existing A → c.
  2. Now A is immediately left recursive with α = a d and β ∈ {b d, c}.
  3. Apply the rule: A → b d A′ | c A′ and A′ → a d A′ | ε.
  4. S itself is not left recursive and stays as it is.

Answer: A → b d A′ | c A′, A′ → a d A′ | ε — option B.

Common misconception. Stopping after the substitution (option A) — the grammar is then still left recursive, only immediately so — or forgetting that the substituted alternative b d also needs the A′ suffix.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: Which one of the following statements about FIRST and FOLLOW sets is FALSE?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following statements about FIRST and FOLLOW sets is FALSE?
options: FOLLOW(A) can contain $ only if A can occur as the rightmost symbol of a sentential form.
If A is nullable and occurs at the end of a production, then FOLLOW(A) contains the FOLLOW of the head of that production.
FIRST(A) contains ε exactly when A is nullable.
FOLLOW(A) contains ε whenever A is nullable.
options_html: FOLLOW(A) can contain $ only if A can occur as the rightmost symbol of a sentential form.
If A is nullable and occurs at the end of a production, then FOLLOW(A) contains the FOLLOW of the head of that production.
FIRST(A) contains ε exactly when A is nullable.
FOLLOW(A) contains ε whenever A is nullable.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. FIRST describes what a string can begin with, and ε is a legitimate "beginning" of a nullable string. FOLLOW describes what can come after a nonterminal in a sentential form; its symbols are always terminals or the end marker $, never ε.

Step by step.

  1. (A) true: $ enters FOLLOW(A) only through the propagation rule for a symbol at the right end of a production, which ultimately traces back to S.
  2. (B) true: this is the standard propagation rule, including the chain through nullable symbols.
  3. (C) true: it is the definition of nullability expressed through FIRST.
  4. (D) false: FOLLOW(A) is a set of terminals and $. Nullability puts ε in FIRST(A) and is handled in the table by copying the ε-production across FOLLOW(A), not by putting ε inside it.

Answer: option D is false.

Common misconception. Symmetry. FIRST and FOLLOW look similar but are asymmetric: FIRST may hold ε, FOLLOW never does; FOLLOW holds $, FIRST never does.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: Which of the following grammars are LL(1)? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Which of the following grammars are LL(1)? (Select all that apply.)
options: S → a S b | ε
S → A a | b, A → b | ε
S → a A | b B, A → c | ε, B → c | ε
E → E + T | T
S → i E t S S′ | a, S′ → e S | ε, E → b
options_html: S → a S b | ε
S → A a | b, A → b | ε
S → a A | b B, A → c | ε, B → c | ε
E → E + T | T
S → i E t S S′ | a, S′ → e S | ε, E → b
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Test each nonterminal: the FIRST sets of its alternatives must be disjoint, and where an alternative is nullable its FOLLOW set must not overlap the FIRST sets of the others. A grammar is LL(1) only if every nonterminal passes.

Step by step.

  1. S → a S b | ε: FIRST sets are {a} and {ε}; FOLLOW(S) = {b, $} does not contain a. LL(1).
  2. S → A a | b with A → b | ε: FIRST(A a) = {b, a} because A can be b or ε, and FIRST(b) = {b}. Both contain b, so M[S, b] gets two entries. Not LL(1).
  3. S → a A | b B, A → c | ε, B → c | ε: FOLLOW(A) = FOLLOW(B) = {$}, so M[A, c] = A → c, M[A, $] = A → ε and likewise for B. The two nonterminals never share a row, so no conflict. LL(1).
  4. E → E + T | T is left recursive: the two alternatives of E have the same FIRST set. Not LL(1).
  5. The dangling-else grammar has two entries in M[S′, e]. Not LL(1).

Answer: options (A) and (C).

Common misconception. Judging by the look of the rules. Option C looks suspicious because A and B have identical right sides, yet it is LL(1): conflicts are per row of the table, and A and B occupy different rows.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: For the grammar S → A B C, A → a | ε, B → b | ε, C → c | ε, how many symbols does FOLLOW(A) contain? Count $ as a symbol. (Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html: For the grammar S → A B C, A → a | ε, B → b | ε, C → c | ε, how many symbols does FOLLOW(A) contain? Count $ as a symbol. (Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. When A is followed by a string of nullable symbols, every terminal that can begin one of them follows A, and if all of them can vanish, the FOLLOW of the head propagates as well.

Step by step.

  1. A occurs in S → A B C, followed by B C.
  2. FIRST(B) − {ε} = {b}, so b ∈ FOLLOW(A).
  3. B is nullable, so FIRST(C) − {ε} = {c} also enters: c ∈ FOLLOW(A).
  4. C is nullable too, so the rest of the right side can vanish completely and FOLLOW(S) = {$} propagates: $ ∈ FOLLOW(A).
  5. FOLLOW(A) = {b, c, $}, three symbols.

Answer: 3 symbols.

Common misconception. Answering 2 by stopping at B, or answering 4 by counting ε. Nullability is what carries the FOLLOW of the head into FOLLOW(A), and ε is never a member of a FOLLOW set.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: In a table-driven predictive parser the symbol on top of the stack is the nonterminal A, the current input symbol is a, and M[A, a] = A → X Y Z. The parser
questions.question_html: In a table-driven predictive parser the symbol on top of the stack is the nonterminal A, the current input symbol is a, and M[A, a] = A → X Y Z. The parser
options: pops A and pushes Z, then Y, then X, so that X is on top.
pops a from the input and pushes A.
shifts a onto the stack.
reduces the handle X Y Z to A.
options_html: pops A and pushes Z, then Y, then X, so that X is on top.
pops a from the input and pushes A.
shifts a onto the stack.
reduces the handle X Y Z to A.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A predictive parser keeps a stack of grammar symbols with the start symbol at the bottom. When the top is a nonterminal it expands it using the table; when the top is a terminal it must match the current input symbol and is popped.

Step by step.

  1. The stack is … A with A on top, so A is popped.
  2. The right side X Y Z is pushed in reverse order — Z first, then Y, then X — so that X, the leftmost symbol, ends up on top and is matched next.
  3. Nothing is consumed from the input at this step; the input pointer moves only when a terminal on top matches.
  4. Options B, C and D describe shift-reduce (bottom-up) behaviour, not predictive parsing.

Answer: option A.

Common misconception. Pushing the right side left to right. That would put Z on top and the parser would try to match the rightmost symbol first — a rightmost, not leftmost, derivation.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: A backtracking recursive-descent parser is used on a grammar with no LL(1) guarantee. In the worst case, for an input of length n, the work it may do grows
questions.question_html: A backtracking recursive-descent parser is used on a grammar with no LL(1) guarantee. In the worst case, for an input of length n, the work it may do grows
options: linearly in n
as n log n
exponentially in n
as n²
options_html: linearly in n
as n log n
exponentially in n
as n²
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A predictive (LL(1)) parser is linear because the table fixes every decision. A backtracking parser instead explores alternatives, and when several alternatives can match the same prefix the number of partial parses can double with every token.

Step by step.

  1. On failure the parser restores the input position and tries the next alternative, re-parsing the same suffix.
  2. If the grammar allows k alternatives at each of n levels, the search tree has on the order of kn nodes.
  3. Classic examples, such as the ambiguous expression grammar, show this exponential blow-up in practice.
  4. Memoisation (packrat parsing) removes the repetition and restores linear time at the cost of memory — but that is no longer plain backtracking.

Answer: exponentially in n — option C.

Common misconception. Assuming any parser is linear in the input. Linearity is a property of the deterministic table-driven method, not of top-down parsing in general.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: Which of the following statements about left recursion and left factoring are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements about left recursion and left factoring are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Left factoring can turn a grammar that is not LL(1) into an LL(1) grammar without changing the language.
Removing left recursion always yields an LL(1) grammar.
Indirect left recursion must be removed by substituting in a fixed order of nonterminals before the immediate left recursion is removed.
A recursive-descent parser that meets a left-recursive alternative recurses forever.
Left factoring introduces no new nonterminals.
options_html: Left factoring can turn a grammar that is not LL(1) into an LL(1) grammar without changing the language.
Removing left recursion always yields an LL(1) grammar.
Indirect left recursion must be removed by substituting in a fixed order of nonterminals before the immediate left recursion is removed.
A recursive-descent parser that meets a left-recursive alternative recurses forever.
Left factoring introduces no new nonterminals.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Left recursion and FIRST/FIRST conflicts are the two obstacles to predictive parsing. Left-recursion elimination removes the first; left factoring removes the second. Neither is a complete LL(1) transformation by itself.

Step by step.

  1. (A) true: a grammar whose only defect is a shared prefix becomes LL(1) after factoring, and factoring preserves the language.
  2. (B) false: S → a A | b B, A → c | ε, B → c | ε is free of left recursion and is LL(1) — but S → A a | b, A → b | ε is also free of left recursion and is not LL(1), because of a FIRST/FIRST conflict.
  3. (C) true: the substitution step turns mutual recursion into immediate recursion, and it needs a fixed order (for example A1, …, An) or the process does not terminate.
  4. (D) true: the procedure for A calls itself before consuming input.
  5. (E) false: factoring creates a new nonterminal (here A′) for every common prefix it extracts.

Answer: options (A), (C) and (D).

Common misconception. Believing "no left recursion" implies "LL(1)". FIRST/FIRST and FIRST/FOLLOW conflicts survive left-recursion removal untouched.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: For the grammar S → A a | b, A → b | ε, which statement about its LL(1) parsing table is TRUE?
questions.question_html: For the grammar S → A a | b, A → b | ε, which statement about its LL(1) parsing table is TRUE?
options: Exactly one cell, M[S, b], holds two entries, so the grammar is not LL(1).
The grammar is LL(1), because the two alternatives of A begin differently.
M[A, a] holds A → b.
M[A, $] holds A → ε.
options_html: Exactly one cell, M[S, b], holds two entries, so the grammar is not LL(1).
The grammar is LL(1), because the two alternatives of A begin differently.
M[A, a] holds A → b.
M[A, $] holds A → ε.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The FIRST set of a right side is computed left to right, and a nullable first symbol lets the following symbols contribute. It is FIRST(A a), not FIRST(A), that decides the row of S.

Step by step.

  1. FIRST(A) = {b, ε}, so FIRST(A a) = {b} ∪ {a} = {b, a}: A may be b, or it may vanish and let a begin the string.
  2. FIRST(b) = {b}, so M[S, b] receives both S → A a and S → b. That is the conflict.
  3. FOLLOW(A) = {a}, so M[A, b] = A → b and M[A, a] = A → ε; M[A, $] stays empty.
  4. So options C and D name cells that hold the wrong entry, and option B ignores the conflict in row S.

Answer: M[S, b] holds two entries — option A.

Common misconception. Checking only the alternatives of the "suspicious" nonterminal A. Here A is perfectly well behaved; the conflict is created one level up, by the nullability of A inside S → A a.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: Which of the following is true of every top-down parser?
questions.question_html: Which of the following is true of every top-down parser?
options: It builds a leftmost derivation of the input string.
It builds a rightmost derivation in reverse.
It reduces handles at the top of the stack.
It can parse every context-free grammar.
options_html: It builds a leftmost derivation of the input string.
It builds a rightmost derivation in reverse.
It reduces handles at the top of the stack.
It can parse every context-free grammar.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A top-down parser starts at the start symbol and expands nonterminals until the frontier matches the input. Expanding the leftmost nonterminal at every step produces a leftmost derivation, so the parse tree grows from the root towards the leaves.

Step by step.

  1. Recursive descent and LL(1) table-driven parsing both expand the leftmost nonterminal, giving a leftmost derivation — statement A.
  2. Statement B describes bottom-up (shift-reduce) parsing, which reconstructs a rightmost derivation in reverse.
  3. Statement C is the handle-reduction step of LR parsing, again bottom-up.
  4. Statement D is false: a top-down parser needs a grammar free of left recursion and FIRST/FIRST conflicts; many context-free grammars, including all ambiguous ones, are outside its reach.

Answer: option A.

Common misconception. Confusing "top-down" with "backtracking" or with "handles". Top-down means root-to-leaves and leftmost expansion; handles and rightmost derivations belong to the bottom-up family.
